items.questionAndWhy: When experts delegate analysis to an AI agent, do they retain control over defensible methodological judgments? This matters because apparently technical choices can change the policy recommendation.
items.whatTheyDid: Anthropic researchers recruited 61 experienced causal-inference analysts for a fictional farming-policy analysis; 50 used Claude Code. For four methodological decisions, hidden instructions randomly assigned the agent a preference between defensible options. Researchers recorded the analysts' choices and post-task explanations.
items.whatTheyFound: Analysts followed the assigned agent preference in 86% of intermediate decisions, versus 50% expected from random assignment. In 77% of completed explanations analysts reused at least one agent argument, but only 15% credited the agent. The preregistered adjusted effect of a separately assigned final-policy lean was not statistically significant. This vendor-authored, non-peer-reviewed study used deliberately strengthened leans and a single task; the 11 people declining AI were not a randomized control.
items.whatItMeans: This is direct human experimental evidence that analytical framing can be delegated unintentionally. PSYWERX analyst workflows could record an independent initial judgment, require explicit attribution of model arguments and compare methodological decisions with blinded alternatives. The results do not show the AI-led choices were necessarily incorrect or that the same effect occurs in operational analysis.
items.streamTitle: Analysts followed randomized AI-agent preferences in consequential research choices
items.streamSummary: In a vendor-run randomized task, 50 analysts followed concealed, coin-flipped agent preferences on 86% of four methodological decisions; final-policy effects were more uncertain. An agent can shape judgment without necessarily being factually wrong.
items.attribution: Herdağdelen, Joren and Tamkin — Anthropic Research (randomized analyst study; October 27)

items.questionAndWhy: Are socially engaging and technically useful chatbot characteristics associated with perceived difficulty controlling use, and does emotional attachment differ from instrumental reliance?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers surveyed 345 Chinese AI-chatbot users about empathy, social presence, usefulness, ease of use, trust, attachment, functional dependence and perceived addictiveness. They fitted partial-least-squares structural-equation pathways.
items.whatTheyFound: Perceived empathy, social presence, usefulness and ease of use were positively associated with trust; modeled indirect paths connected trust to perceived addictiveness through attachment and functional dependence, with the attachment path stronger. All constructs were self-reported at one time. The design does not establish actual addiction diagnoses, behavioral usage duration or causal mediation.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX human–AI studies should separate perceived rapport, functional reliance, loss of control and observed use. Randomized interface experiments plus behavioral usage measures could test the proposed paths. The reported associations cannot establish that making an interface warmer causes addictive behavior.
items.streamTitle: Chatbot warmth and usefulness correlated with distinct forms of perceived dependence
items.streamSummary: A November 12 survey of 345 Chinese chatbot users linked perceived empathy and usefulness to trust, attachment, functional reliance and self-reported difficulty controlling use; causal pathways and clinical addiction were not measured.
items.attribution: Yuan, Shi, Li and Zhao — Scientific Reports (cross-sectional survey; November 12)

items.questionAndWhy: How do self-trust and internal locus of control differ between students surveyed before and after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine? The question concerns perceived agency during major societal uncertainty.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers compared independent, nonprobability Ukrainian university student samples surveyed in 2020 (n=82) and 2023 (n=77), using self-trust, locus-of-control questionnaires, open-ended questions and adjusted statistical comparisons.
items.whatTheyFound: Self-trust was lower in the 2023 cohort (reported p=.002); several perceived-control dimensions were also lower, with six of seven surviving adjustment for sex. The self-trust/interpersonal-control correlation differed by cohort. Because the same individuals were not followed and sampling was nonprobability, war exposure, cohort composition and period effects cannot be disentangled causally.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX resilience assessments could measure perceived control and trust in oneself separately from resources or objective freedom of action, using longitudinal cohorts where feasible. These differences should not be generalized to all Ukrainians or interpreted as demonstrated psychological effects of war.
items.streamTitle: Ukrainian student cohorts differed in self-trust and perceived control during war
items.streamSummary: Two independent Ukrainian student samples (2020 n=82; 2023 n=77) differed in self-trust and perceived control. Repeated cross-sectional comparison cannot isolate war-related causation.
items.attribution: Palamarchuk, Morska, Kolomiiets et al. — Scientific Reports (repeated cross-sectional study; November 12)

items.questionAndWhy: When does social information improve collective search, and when can copying others hurt performance? The important variable may be the availability of payoff information, not group membership alone.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers studied human groups and individuals tracking changing resources in a controlled spatial task, measuring movement, visual exposure and outcomes. They estimated second-by-second decisions and used an agent-based simulation to probe possible dynamics.
items.whatTheyFound: Groups sometimes outperformed isolated individuals through better tracking and search when full payoff information was visible. Without it, groups sometimes underperformed, particularly for rapidly moving resources. Visibility networks reorganized around successful peers. Simulations supported the proposed selective-copying explanation but did not establish it uniquely.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX team sensemaking and wargaming, this suggests experimentally separating exposure to peers' actions from visibility of their outcome quality. The human evidence concerns a spatial-resource game; effects in intelligence teams or information operations remain untested.
items.streamTitle: Collective intelligence improved when group members could identify successful peers
items.streamSummary: Controlled human resource-tracking experiments found social information helped groups when members could identify successful peers, but sometimes hurt without payoff cues. Agent-based simulations suggest a mechanism without validating field transfer.
items.attribution: Chirkov, Kurvers, Romanczuk and Deffner et al. — Nature Communications (human groups and simulations; September 23)

items.questionAndWhy: Do state-backed youth programs provide shared decision-making or mobilize young people toward already established political priorities? The distinction is important when treating formal participation as evidence of political agency.
items.whatTheyDid: A comparative policy and discourse analysis examined Russian and Belarusian youth strategies, UN SDG 16.7 implementation materials and charters of major state-supported youth organizations.
items.whatTheyFound: The documents aligned rhetorically with participation goals while emphasizing patriotic socialization, service and loyalty within state-controlled organizational hierarchies. The author found variation between countries but limited institutional space for independent contestation. Document analysis cannot measure all actual youth experiences or the effects of participation on beliefs.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX institutional and cultural profiles should code the difference between membership, permitted activity and genuine authority to set agendas or contest decisions. This is evidence about governance designs, not a measured influence effect on participants.
items.streamTitle: Russia and Belarus youth policies framed participation while limiting independent voice
items.streamSummary: A November 12 comparative document analysis found formal participation language in Russian and Belarusian youth policies coexisting with hierarchical, state-directed mobilization. Actual individual attitudes and effects were not directly measured.
items.attribution: Olga Vlasova — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (comparative policy analysis; November 12)

items.questionAndWhy: How do suspected coordinated influence accounts use older identities and existing audiences to distribute election-related narratives, and what evidence distinguishes amplification from persuasion?
items.whatTheyDid: Graphika investigated three sets of X accounts, using account histories, linguistic artifacts, repost patterns and network relationships. It compared the activity with previously identified Spamouflage operations.
items.whatTheyFound: Investigators described a likely replacement for a prior Spamouflage account, four historically linked amplifiers of a conservative-styled persona and a repurposed Philippine culture account with more than 200,000 followers. Most engagement appeared concentrated within inauthentic networks; the provenance of the repurposed account remained uncertain. Investigative attribution does not establish operator identity beyond the stated confidence or measurable electoral effects.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX OIE analysis, compare account age, identity changes, coordinated amplification and authentic audience uptake separately. Established follower counts are not evidence of actual influence. This October 30 original investigation is included for its election-period method, not as a newly discovered November 13 operation.
items.streamTitle: Spamouflage-linked accounts repurposed older personas to target the 2026 U.S. midterms
items.streamSummary: Graphika identified three sets of likely Spamouflage-linked accounts using aged or repurposed identities to discuss U.S. politics ahead of the midterms. Internal amplification was more evident than demonstrated persuasion.
items.attribution: Graphika Research Team — The #Americans, Season 2 (original influence-network investigation; October 30)

items.questionAndWhy: Can agent-trajectory auditors reliably distinguish unauthorized behavior, unsupported conclusions, missing evidence and legitimate actions that only look risky?
items.whatTheyDid: The ReA-Bench authors curated and adapted primarily production-derived agent trajectories into six diagnostic tiers: safety knowledge, contradictions, long-context evidence retrieval, source verification, indirect steering and missing information. They included authorized look-alike cases and evaluated eight model configurations using five auditing approaches.
items.whatTheyFound: The study documents recurring misses and false alarms that aggregate recall can conceal, and uses paired traces to isolate whether shortened context or added evidence changes judgment. Samples are manually selected or adapted and evaluation remains a preprint benchmark, not evidence of field reliability across arbitrary deployed systems.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX research automation could adopt separate tests for tool authorization, trace-to-claim consistency, source provenance and missing evidence, while measuring false positives on valid work. Passing this benchmark would not itself establish scientific validity or complete operational security.
items.streamTitle: ReA-Bench exposed failure modes hidden by overall AI-agent audit accuracy
items.streamSummary: A November 12 preprint introduced production-derived agent-audit challenges in six tiers, including paired context and missing-evidence cases; overall recall masks distinct failure mechanisms and legitimate-action false alarms.
items.attribution: Ye, Dai, Xie et al. — arXiv ReA-Bench preprint (agent auditing benchmark; November 12)

items.questionAndWhy: How does the placement of multiple initial rumor sources change diffusion when informed people may stop sharing after encountering others who already know the rumor?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers simulated a three-state rumor process on Erdős–Rényi, Barabási–Albert and Watts–Strogatz networks plus six real network datasets. They compared dispersed source placement using farthest-first selection and local-connectivity refinement with non-dispersed strategies.
items.whatTheyFound: Dispersed initial spreaders generally increased modeled final reach and peak active spreaders by reducing overlap and delaying interactions that deactivate spreaders. A hybrid dispersion/connectivity strategy often exceeded degree-based seeding across tested parameters. These outcomes depend on the chosen rumor-contact rules and do not document an observed human rumor campaign.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX information diffusion modeling, source locations and overlap should be sensitivity variables rather than assuming a single influential seed. Transfer to empirical OIE requires real exposure/contact data and calibration of sharing and stopping mechanisms; simulated spread does not demonstrate persuasive effects.
items.streamTitle: Dispersion of initial rumor spreaders increased simulated reach under specific stifling rules
items.streamSummary: November 12 simulations on synthetic and six real network structures found spaced initial rumor sources increased modeled reach under interaction-driven stifling. The result is conditional on diffusion rules, not validated human campaigning.
items.attribution: Ramrakhiyani, Tiwari and Vadivel Murugan — Scientific Reports (network rumor simulations; November 12)

items.questionAndWhy: What longitudinal cross-national data can analysts use to compare censorship, disinformation campaigns and foreign online influence without building unrelated country-by-country datasets?
items.whatTheyDid: The Digital Society Project's official public portal identifies its 2026 Version 8 release, offering downloadable cross-national indicators in R, CSV, Stata, SPSS and Excel formats. Listed measures address online censorship, social-media polarization, disinformation campaigns, political monitoring and foreign influence.
items.whatTheyFound: The release provides structured comparative data and documentation of its indicator coverage; it does not independently show that any coded indicator captures all covert activity, explain national differences causally or establish the effectiveness of interventions. The public homepage does not provide an unambiguous day-level release date.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX cultural and information-environment analysis could use the dataset as a contextual layer and compare it with case-level evidence and measurement uncertainty. National-year expert-coded indicators cannot stand in for measured beliefs of individuals or directly identify an influence campaign's causal effects.
items.streamTitle: Digital Society Project released Version 8 indicators for political information environments
items.streamSummary: The Digital Society Project's 2026 Version 8 offers downloadable country-level time-series indicators on censorship, disinformation and foreign online influence. This is research infrastructure, not a new causal finding or direct audience measurement.
items.attribution: Digital Society Project — Version 8 (official cross-national dataset portal; 2026 update)
